title: What Are State-Space Models?
hook: A compact hidden state summarizes everything seen so far - update it with each new input and you get sequence modeling that scales linearly, not quadratically.
key_points: Borrowed from control theory: a system evolves via two equations - one updates hidden state, one produces output.
Processing a sequence is linear in length, unlike Transformer self-attention which is quadratic.
The same model can run as a recurrence (step-by-step) for inference or as a convolution (parallelized) for training.
The hidden state is fixed-size, so memory cost does not grow with sequence length during inference.
content_html: State-space models (SSMs) come from control theory, where they describe how a dynamical system evolves over time using a hidden state vector. Researchers in deep learning have adapted the idea into sequence models that can handle very long inputs more cheaply than Transformers.
extra_html:
How it works

An SSM defines two linear equations: the state equation updates a hidden vector h using the current input and a transition matrix A, and the output equation produces the model's prediction from h. With the right parameterization, the recurrence can be "unrolled" into a convolution over the input sequence - allowing fully parallel training while reverting to the recurrent form at inference time. This dual mode is what makes SSMs attractive: training speed close to attention, inference cost close to an RNN.

Why it matters

Quadratic attention cost becomes a real bottleneck at context lengths in the tens of thousands. SSMs sidestep this, making long documents, audio, and genomics sequences tractable. S4 and Mamba are the most prominent deep-learning SSMs; starting with the Wikipedia article on state-space representation gives you the mathematical backbone before diving into either.

related.title: S4: Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces
related.hook: A clever matrix parameterization turns the notoriously unstable state-space recurrence into a stable, fast sequence model that handles sequences 100x longer than Transformers.

related.title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
related.hook: Make the state-space transitions depend on the input itself, add a hardware-aware scan, and you get a linear-time sequence model that matches Transformers on language - with no KV cache.

related.title: RNNs, LSTMs & Sequences
related.hook: To read a sequence, a network can loop over it one step at a time, carrying a memory of what came before. Plain RNNs forget fast; LSTMs add gates so they remember longer.

flashcards.prompt: What two equations define a state-space model?
flashcards.back_html: A state equation that updates a hidden vector from the current input, and an output equation that produces the prediction from that state.

flashcards.prompt: How does an SSM's compute cost scale with sequence length, versus self-attention?

choices.text: Linear in length, whereas self-attention is quadratic

flashcards.explanation_html: Processing a sequence is linear in length for SSMs, unlike the quadratic cost of Transformer self-attention.

flashcards.prompt: Why can the same SSM train fast yet infer cheaply?

choices.text: It runs as a parallelizable convolution for training and a recurrence for inference
It uses a different set of weights for each mode
It grows its hidden state with the sequence at inference

flashcards.explanation_html: The dual mode - convolution for parallel training, recurrence with a fixed-size state for inference - gives both benefits.
